3.title: Scopes & Symbol Tables
3.lead: Resolve names correctly, preserve outer scopes and trace lookup, bind, enter and exit.
sections: Names and lexical scope

A declaration associates a name with an item. A scope is the region where it is visible. The closest enclosing declaration wins. Lexical scoping depends on the program structure, not the current execution call path.
The five operations
empty creates a table; bind adds a binding; lookup finds the most recent applicable binding or reports unbound; enter starts a nested scope; exit restores the previous scope.
Persistent vs imperative
Persistent tables retain old versions, so restoration uses the saved reference. Imperative tables mutate shared state and must record the changes needed for undoing a scope.
Persistent list representation
empty is []; bind prepends (name,info); lookup scans front to back; enter remembers the old list reference; exit restores that reference. This naturally supports shadowing.
Imperative stack representation
empty is an empty stack; bind pushes a pair; lookup searches top-down; enter pushes a marker; exit pops back through the nearest marker.
Efficiency
List/stack lookup is worst-case linear in number of bindings. Hashing commonly gives approximately constant-time lookup; scope restoration still needs an undo strategy.
Namespaces
Some languages use separate namespaces for variables and functions; others share them. Separate tables or tagged names implement separate namespaces.

4.title: Interpretation
4.lead: Evaluate an abstract syntax tree by recursion: expressions return runtime values, not types or code.
sections: Structure of an interpreter

An interpreter has a function per syntactic category. Each takes an AST subtree and inherited environments, then returns a value or other output. The example language from Grammar 4.1 uses integers, Booleans, functions and let expressions.
Example language

Programs are function declarations, with main : (int)→int. Expressions include numbers, variables, addition, less-than, conditionals, function calls and let bindings. Addition accepts integers only; comparisons accept equal types.
EvalExp and EvalExps
EvalExp(Exp,vtable,ftable) returns an integer or Boolean. vtable stores variable VALUES; ftable maps functions to declaration syntax trees. EvalExps returns an ordered list of values.
Calling functions
Evaluate argument expressions, check arity and types, create a new parameter→value environment, evaluate the function body, then validate its result against the declared type.
Whole program
Build the table of all function declarations, look up main, and call it with the integer program input.
Interpretation vs compilation
An interpreter directly examines AST nodes during execution and may repeat checks. A compiler generally translates ahead of time. Both are implementation strategies; neither has to follow the other.

5.title: Type Checking
5.lead: Propagate environments down and types up; report errors while retaining the textbook’s recovery conventions.
sections: Static/dynamic and strong/weak
Static checks occur before execution, dynamic at runtime. Strong/weak concerns how strongly types constrain operations. Figure 5.1 illustrates the conceptual design space.
Attributes
Inherited attributes flow into subtrees (e.g. vtable, ftable); synthesised attributes flow up (e.g. expression type). Information may switch roles between subtrees/passes.
Environments
vtable maps variables to TYPES (int,bool), ftable maps functions to types such as (int,bool)→int. Symbol tables are assumed persistent.
CheckExp and CheckExps
CheckExp(Exp,vtable,ftable) applies Figure 5.2. It returns a type, and error() REPORTS but does not stop the checker. CheckExps returns a type list.
CheckFun / CheckTypeIds
Build local parameter type environment; reject duplicate names; check body and compare its type with declared result. GetTypeId extracts one name/type pair.
CheckProgram: two passes
Pass 1 builds ftable for ALL functions, supporting mutual recursion. Pass 2 checks bodies. Check that main : (int)→int and there are no duplicate function declarations.
Advanced checking
Assignments, structured data, overloading, explicit/implicit conversions, polymorphism, and inferred types all extend the core type-checking ideas.
Exercises and recovery
Figure 5.2 can return a guessed type even after error(). Exercise 5.3 adds an unknown type to reduce cascaded false error messages.

6.title: Intermediate-Code Generation
6.lead: Generate executable intermediate instructions using recursive syntax-directed translation and explicit destinations/labels.
sections: Intermediate language
The intermediate language uses simple operations, assignments, jumps, labels and function-oriented instructions. Figure 6.1 is the authoritative instruction inventory.
Syntax-directed translation
Translation is driven by AST forms. Recursive functions take AST fragments and inherited context and return code lists. Parent code is assembled in precisely the rule-specified order.
TransExp
Expression translation takes expression and destination, allocates temporaries using newvar, translates children and emits operations. Figure 6.3 contains the rules.
TransStat
Assignments, sequences, if, while and repeat/until use TransExp/TransCond and label allocation. Figure 6.5 supplies the exact code layout.
TransCond and logical operators
Conditions translate to control flow instead of necessarily producing a boolean value. Figure 6.6 covers simple conditions and Figure 6.8 short-circuit and/or.
Advanced control statements
Break, continue and other constructs require inherited jump destinations and careful scope for labels.
Structured data
Arrays require address calculations, dimensions and scaling; strings, floating-point and records need representation-aware translation. Figures 6.9–6.11 supply array patterns.
Declarations
Generate code or storage information for locals and function declarations; Figure 6.12 describes simple declarations.
Practice strategy
Allocate resources when the rule says to allocate; recursively finish children; concatenate code fragments in the prescribed order—allocation order and emission order differ.

9.title: Functions & Activation Records
9.lead: Understand how generated function calls use the stack, registers and machine-level calling conventions.
sections: The call stack
A function call creates activation-specific runtime state. Calls nest in LIFO order. The newest active invocation is at the top; recursion creates multiple frames for one function.
Activation records
A frame may hold arguments, saved registers, return address and local values according to the calling convention. Figure 9.1 defines the book’s simple frame layout.
Prologues, epilogues, call sequences
Caller prepares and enters the call; callee prologue establishes a frame; epilogue restores state and returns. Figures 9.2–9.4 show exact sequences for the simple layout.
Callee saves registers
A callee-preservation convention saves selected registers in the function being called, then restores them. See Figures 9.5–9.8.
Caller-saves versus callee-saves
Under caller-saves, the caller protects values it needs after the call; under callee-saves, the callee preserves agreed registers. The split affects efficiency and allocation.
Registers and allocator interaction
Arguments and return values can be passed via registers. Call-convention constraints and register allocation must agree; Figures 9.9–9.13 cover one division.
Local variables
Variables may reside in registers or on the stack depending on lifetime, address-taking and register pressure.
Non-local variables
Globals, call-by-reference and nested scope access introduce addressing beyond simple local registers.
Functions as parameters and variants
Function pointers/closures, variable-sized stack frames, varargs and alternative stack directions affect layout and conventions.
Optimisations
Inlining substitutes function bodies at call sites, requiring capture-avoiding renaming. Tail-call optimisation can reuse activation state when correct.
